options: The parameter items has no type annotation and cannot be inferred, causing TypeScript to implicitly fall back to any, which --noImplicitAny rejects.
The property .length is not recognized unless the array element type is explicitly defined.
Functions must always declare an explicit return type whenever --noImplicitAny is enabled.
Parameters that access collection properties must declare a generic interface constraint.
quiz.explanation: When type annotations are missing and TypeScript cannot infer a variable or parameter type, it defaults to type any. Enabling --noImplicitAny turns this implicit fallback into a compiler error. TypeScript can still infer the return type of items.length as number, so the return type is not what triggers the error.
quiz.objective: Identify type errors triggered by --noImplicitAny and --strictNullChecks when handling unannotated variables and nullish values

quiz.stem: A function signature is defined as `function getLength(str: string | null): number`. When `--strictNullChecks` is enabled, why does the expression `return str.length;` inside the function body trigger a compiler error?
options: Under --strictNullChecks, null has its own distinct type and cannot be used where a concrete value of type string is expected without checking first.
The string type in TypeScript does not have a built-in .length property unless asserted with the as operator.
Enabling --strictNullChecks completely forbids union types containing null from being passed as function parameters.
TypeScript requires undefined to always be included whenever null is specified in a parameter union type.
quiz.explanation: When strictNullChecks is true, null and undefined have their own distinct types and cause type errors if used where a concrete value is expected. Because str can be null, dereferencing .length is unsafe until str is checked or narrowed. Union types containing null are allowed, but the null case must be handled explicitly.
quiz.objective: Identify type errors triggered by --noImplicitAny and --strictNullChecks when handling unannotated variables and nullish values

lessons.title: Configuring tsconfig.json and Target Downleveling
lessons.recall: In the previous lesson, you learned how TypeScript uses type annotations to verify values and handle nullable types before code executes. You also saw how type checking catches type mismatches and prevents runtime errors in basic functions.
lessons.explanation:
A `tsconfig.json` file designates the root files and compiler options needed to compile a TypeScript project [c:16ba0688280d]. When `compilerOptions` is omitted from `tsconfig.json`, TypeScript applies default compiler settings [c:615704781761]. Running `tsc` locally without arguments compiles the nearest project defined by a `tsconfig.json` file [c:b33de842c7a5]. If you invoke `tsc` without specifying input files, the compiler searches for `tsconfig.json` starting in the current directory and continues up through parent directories [c:85a2c118de03]. You can also invoke `tsc` with the `--project` or `-p` flag pointing to a directory or a specific configuration file to compile a project [c:362b300dcb2e]. In contrast, specifying input files directly on the command line causes `tsc` to ignore `tsconfig.json` files entirely [c:8d83ae64703a] [c:1bdac63c0513].

Setting `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json` turns on all strict mode family options simultaneously [c:264420167f31] [c:66675914e5a9]. Enabling the strict flag enforces stronger guarantees of program correctness across the codebase [c:4d80a795b4d2]. Even when `strict` is set to `true`, individual strict mode family checks can be turned off independently if needed [c:264420167f31] [c:e39da5a43491].

The `target` compiler option specifies the JavaScript language version for emitted JavaScript and includes corresponding compatible library declarations [c:7886e528a1aa]. Downleveling allows TypeScript to rewrite and transpile newer ECMAScript syntax to older ECMAScript versions based on this target [c:88f58fa8dded]. For instance, setting `target` to `es2015` compiles TypeScript code down to ECMAScript 2015 compatible code so it runs anywhere ECMAScript 2015 is supported [c:f20e1f15ea50].

exercise.task: Configure `tsconfig.json` to enable strict mode and project compilation downleveling to ECMAScript 2015. Specifically, set `compilerOptions.target` to `"es2015"` and `compilerOptions.strict` to `true`.
hints: Look at `tsconfig.json` inside the `compilerOptions` block.
Change `"target": "TODO_TARGET"` to `"target": "es2015"`.
Set `"strict": true` instead of `"strict": false`.

quiz.stem: A team has a project containing a valid `tsconfig.json` file in the project root. A developer runs `tsc src/index.ts` from that root directory. Why does TypeScript report unexpected errors or ignore settings defined in `tsconfig.json`?
options: Passing input files directly on the command line causes tsc to ignore tsconfig.json configuration files.
The compiler requires passing the -p flag whenever an individual file is located inside a subdirectory.
TypeScript only parses tsconfig.json if the command is executed with sudo or administrator privileges.
A tsconfig.json file can only be detected when input files are provided through stdin.
quiz.explanation: Passing input files directly on the command line causes tsc to ignore tsconfig.json configuration files. To compile using tsconfig.json, run tsc without input file arguments or pass the --project (-p) option. Options mentioning administrator privileges, stdin, or requiring -p for subdirectories do not reflect how tsc handles command-line arguments.
quiz.objective: Write a tsconfig.json file enabling strict mode and project compilation

quiz.stem: You need to compile modern TypeScript code so that the emitted JavaScript runs on an environment that only supports ECMAScript 2015. Which configuration option achieves this downleveling in `tsconfig.json`?
options: "compilerOptions": { "target": "es2015" }
"compilerOptions": { "downlevel": "es2015" }
"compilerOptions": { "ecmaVersion": 2015 }
"compilerOptions": { "outputSyntax": "es6-compatible" }
quiz.explanation: The target compiler option specifies the ECMAScript language version for emitted JavaScript, and setting it to es2015 downlevels newer syntax to ECMAScript 2015. Options such as downlevel, ecmaVersion, or outputSyntax are not valid TypeScript compiler options.
quiz.objective: Configure the target compiler option to downlevel modern JavaScript syntax to ECMAScript 2015

quiz.stem: What is the effect of configuring `"strict": true` inside `compilerOptions` in a `tsconfig.json` file?
options: It activates all strict mode family options at once to provide stronger guarantees of program correctness.
It prevents JavaScript files from being emitted whenever any warning occurs during compilation.
It forbids importing modules from external packages outside the local directory.
It restricts TypeScript to running only on ECMAScript 3 compatible runtime environments.
quiz.explanation: Setting strict: true activates all strict mode family options simultaneously, giving stronger guarantees of program correctness. It does not restrict runtime environments to ES3, prevent external module imports, or unconditionally block output for warnings.
quiz.objective: Write a tsconfig.json file enabling strict mode and project compilation

lessons.title: Interfaces, Type Aliases, and Property Modifiers
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons established how TypeScript checks primitive types such as string and number, and how strict null checks guard against null or undefined values. We also saw how functions declare parameter and return types to make expected values explicit.
lessons.explanation:
Object types are defined by listing their properties along with their types [c:3efccaa03a6f]. In TypeScript, object types can be named using an interface declaration or a type alias [c:9a530cef2743]. An interface declaration serves as a way to define and name an object type [c:c88df3660414]. Interfaces fill the role of naming types and defining contracts within code as well as contracts with external code [c:76e5739f67d5]. However, interfaces can only declare object shapes and cannot be used to rename primitives [c:e5a72c246241]. When checking an interface, the type checker does not require properties to match any specific order, as long as the required properties are present and match their required types [c:7ea665197165].

Properties can be marked as optional in object types by appending a question mark (?) after the property name [c:74aee2ca7a02]. Optional properties on an interface are declared by placing a ? at the end of the property name in the declaration [c:1c6b04be0055]. Properties can also be marked as optional by appending a ? to their names in type aliases [c:aac64643e71c]. When strictNullChecks is enabled, reading from an optional property will indicate that its value is potentially undefined [c:42df82019cea].

To restrict property modification, the const keyword is used for immutable variables, whereas readonly is used for immutable properties [c:e0731bda189b]. Marking an object property with the readonly modifier prevents reassignment to that property during type-checking [c:effc5232b8de]. The readonly modifier prevents re-writing the property itself, but it does not make nested object contents immutable [c:a46bf823c824]. Furthermore, TypeScript does not consider readonly modifiers when evaluating compatibility between types, meaning readonly properties can change value via aliasing [c:0f23963ff3b5].

exercise.task:
Define data contracts for a web application in `models.ts`:

1. Export an interface `User` with:
   - `readonly id: number`
   - `username: string`
   - `email: string`
   - `bio?: string` (optional)
   - `avatarUrl?: string` (optional)

2. Export a type alias `Post` with:
   - `readonly id: number`
   - `readonly authorId: number`
   - `title: string`
   - `content: string`

3. Export `formatUserProfile(user: User): string` which returns `"<username> (<email>): <bio>"` if `user.bio` is present, or `"<username> (<email>)"` if `user.bio` is undefined.

4. Export `formatPostPreview(post: Post): string` which returns `"[Post #<id> by <authorId>] <title>"`.
hints: Use 'interface User { ... }' for the user declaration, and 'type Post = { ... }' for the post declaration.
Prepend 'readonly' before 'id' (and 'authorId') to prevent reassignment, and append '?' after 'bio' and 'avatarUrl' to mark them optional.
In formatUserProfile, check 'if (user.bio !== undefined)' to choose between including ': ' + user.bio or just the username and email.

quiz.stem: A developer wants to define a contract for an API response representing a product entity with an id, title, and price. They also want to define a shorthand name for an ID primitive that can be either string or number. Which TypeScript declaration strategy should they choose?
options: Use an interface or type alias for the product object, and a type alias for the primitive ID shorthand.
Use an interface for both the product object and the primitive ID shorthand.
Use an interface for the primitive ID shorthand, but a type alias for the product object.
Use the const keyword to declare both the product shape and the primitive ID shorthand.
quiz.explanation: Object types can be named using either an interface declaration or a type alias, but interfaces can only declare object shapes and cannot rename primitives. Therefore, the primitive ID shorthand must use a type alias. The option suggesting an interface for both is wrong because interfaces cannot rename primitives. The option suggesting an interface for the primitive shorthand is backwards for the same reason. The option suggesting const confuses runtime variable declaration with type declarations.
quiz.objective: Define application entity shapes using interface declarations and type aliases

options: The compiler rejects account.id = 'new-id' during type-checking, and treats account.nickname as potentially undefined.
The compiler allows account.id = 'new-id' at compile time, but throws a runtime TypeError when modifying the property.
The compiler rejects account.id = 'new-id', but treats account.nickname as strictly string because undefined is stripped.
The compiler allows account.id = 'new-id' if account was declared with let, and treats nickname as string | null.
quiz.explanation: Marking a property with readonly prevents reassignment to that property during type-checking, and under strictNullChecks reading an optional property indicates that its value is potentially undefined. The option claiming a runtime TypeError is wrong because readonly does not change runtime behavior. The option claiming undefined is stripped is wrong because optional properties include undefined. The option claiming let allows property reassignment is wrong because readonly applies to the property itself regardless of variable declaration.
quiz.objective: Apply optional (?) and readonly modifiers to object properties to prevent unwanted reassignment and support optional fields

options: TypeScript forbids reassigning list.tags = [], but permits mutating list.tags.push('javascript').
TypeScript forbids both reassigning list.tags = [] and mutating list.tags.push('javascript').
TypeScript permits reassigning list.tags = [] because list was declared with const.
TypeScript converts tags into a runtime-frozen array that throws on list.tags.push('javascript').
quiz.explanation: The readonly modifier prevents re-writing the property itself during type-checking, but it does not make nested object contents immutable. Therefore, list.tags = [] is rejected, but mutating the array via list.tags.push('javascript') is allowed. The option stating both are forbidden is a common misconception that readonly deeply freezes objects. The option stating reassigning is permitted confuses variable bindings with property modifiers. The option claiming runtime freezing is wrong because readonly has no runtime effect.
quiz.objective: Apply optional (?) and readonly modifiers to object properties to prevent unwanted reassignment and support optional fields

lessons.title: Composing Shapes with Inheritance and Intersections
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons established how to describe object shapes using interfaces and type aliases, including optional and readonly modifiers. We also saw how union types let values accept one of several possible types.
lessons.explanation:
Interfaces can extend other interfaces using the `extends` keyword to copy members and compose shapes into reusable components [c:5785ba19c85b]. The `extends` keyword allows an interface to copy and build upon members from other named types, adding whatever new members are needed [c:bdca79e8fb87] [c:ccf66434a0be]. An interface can also extend multiple types simultaneously [c:83c76fac3ad9]. Extending interfaces with `extends` is often more performant for the compiler than composing type aliases with intersections [c:411f8d2dbede].

TypeScript also provides intersection types to combine existing object types using the `&` operator [c:bb8f1d731530] [c:abcd7b92d338]. When you intersect two or more types, the resulting type contains all the properties of every constituent type [c:bb8f1d731530].

When intersecting types have conflicting property types, the conflicting property types are merged automatically [c:36fc31dcd1de]. TypeScript expects the property to satisfy both types simultaneously, which can result in the property having type `never` [c:36fc31dcd1de]. For instance, if type `A` has an `id: string` and type `B` has an `id: number`, the intersection `A & B` yields an `id` property of type `string & number`, which collapses to `never` because no value can be both a string and a number simultaneously [c:36fc31dcd1de].

exercise.task:
In `models.ts`:
1. Define and export an interface `Timestamped` containing `createdAt: Date` and `updatedAt: Date`.
2. Update `User` and `Post` so that both inherit from `Timestamped` using `extends`.
3. Define and export types `Permission` and `AuditDetails`, then compose them into `AdminRole` using the `&` intersection operator.
   - `Permission` must have `role: string` and `canDelete: boolean`.
   - `AuditDetails` must have `lastLogin: Date`.
4. Define and export a type `ConflictingId` that intersects `{ id: string } & { id: number }`, and export a type alias `ConflictCheck = ConflictingId['id']` which collapses to `never`.
5. Implement and export `createAuditedUser(user: User, admin: AdminRole)` which returns a merged object containing all properties of `user` and `admin`.
hints: Use `interface User extends Timestamped` to inherit common date properties.
Combine `Permission` and `AuditDetails` using the `&` operator: `export type AdminRole = Permission & AuditDetails;`.
In TypeScript, intersecting `{ id: string } & { id: number }` forces `id` to be `string & number`, which resolves to `never`.

options: interface Person extends Named, Aged {}
interface Person implements Named, Aged {}
interface Person = Named & Aged;
interface Person extends (Named & Aged) {}
quiz.explanation: `interface Person extends Named, Aged {}` is correct because an interface can extend multiple types simultaneously using comma separation. `implements` is used by classes to adhere to an interface, not by interfaces extending other interfaces. `interface Person = Named & Aged;` is invalid syntax because `interface` cannot use `=` assignment.
quiz.objective: Compose object shapes using interface extends and type intersection (&)

options: never
string | number
number
any
quiz.explanation: When intersecting types have conflicting property types, the conflicting properties are merged into an intersection `string & number`. Because no value can be both a string and a number simultaneously, TypeScript collapses the property type to `never`. It does not create a union `string | number` nor does it let one override the other.
quiz.objective: Predict type conflicts resulting in never when intersecting types with incompatible property definitions

quiz.stem: Why might a development team prefer `interface Child extends Parent` over `type Child = Parent & { ... }` when composing object shapes in a large project?
options: Extending interfaces using the extends keyword is often more performant for the compiler than composing type aliases with intersections.
Type intersections with `&` cannot combine two object types that have different property names.
Interfaces can only extend classes, while type intersections can only combine primitive types.
Interfaces automatically prevent any two properties from having the same name, while intersections always compile without checking.
quiz.explanation: Using interfaces with `extends` can often be more performant for the compiler than type aliases with intersections. Intersections can combine object types with different property names, and interfaces extend types or interfaces, not just classes.
quiz.objective: Compose object shapes using interface extends and type intersection (&)

lessons.title: Index Signatures and Excess Property Checks
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons showed how to define object interfaces and type aliases with explicit and optional properties. We also saw how TypeScript checks types structurally rather than nominally.
lessons.explanation:
When working with dictionary-like structures such as HTTP headers or custom settings, property names may not be known ahead of time, but the value shape is known [c:f6c6cab2c11c]. In these cases, you can use an index signature to describe the types of possible values [c:f6c6cab2c11c]. TypeScript limits index signature properties to `string`, `number`, `symbol`, template string patterns, or union types consisting purely of these types [c:2742afec9c92, c:07f671215525]. An index signature can also be marked `readonly` to disallow assignment to indexed properties [c:821369637639].

A string index signature enforces that all explicitly defined properties in the interface match the index signature's return type [c:54f090d249b2, c:7c3833b8cc46]. In addition, when using both numeric and string indexers on the same type, the return type of the numeric indexer must be a subtype of the type returned by the string indexer [c:83244bbef00b, c:0e9dddd6914b].

Object literals receive special treatment in TypeScript: assigning an object literal to a variable or passing it as an argument triggers excess property checking [c:af4de9ab3143, c:e3fb2a83dc5f]. If the object literal has any properties that the target type does not specify, the compiler produces an error [c:af4de9ab3143, c:e3fb2a83dc5f].

There are two primary ways to resolve excess property checking errors when extra properties are legitimate. First, adding a string index signature to the target interface allows the type to accept arbitrary extra properties without error [c:982b0105d839, c:6c4e48b9386d]. Second, assigning the object literal to an intermediate variable before passing it bypasses excess property checks, provided the object shares at least one common property with the target type [c:77abb5b07ae1, c:5a43571d92a2]. Excess property checks can also be bypassed using a type assertion [c:693829d8513e].

exercise.task:
In `http.ts`, define two dictionary interfaces and two helper functions for an HTTP client:
1. Define `HttpHeaders` as an interface that has an explicit optional property `contentType?: string` and a string index signature returning `string | undefined` so arbitrary headers can be set.
2. Define `RequestOptions` as an interface with `url: string`, `method?: string`, and `headers?: HttpHeaders`. To allow arbitrary custom request options without triggering excess property checks, include a string index signature returning `unknown`.
3. Implement `buildHeaders(customHeaders: Record<string, string>): HttpHeaders` which merges `{ contentType: 'application/json' }` with `customHeaders`.
4. Implement `sendWithIntermediate(options: { url: string; debugToken: string }): { url: string; method: string }` which assigns its argument to an intermediate variable and passes it to `createRequest` (a function that expects `SimpleRequestOptions` without `debugToken`), returning the result.
hints: To add a string index signature to an interface, use `[key: string]: ReturnType;` inside the interface definition.
In `HttpHeaders`, remember that explicit properties like `contentType?: string` must match the index signature's return type `string | undefined`.
In `sendWithIntermediate`, store the incoming parameter in an intermediate variable (`const intermediate = options;`) and pass that variable to `createRequest`.

quiz.stem: You have an interface with a string index signature: `interface Dictionary { [key: string]: number; id: string; }`. Why does the TypeScript compiler reject this definition?
options: String index signatures cannot be used on interfaces that have named properties.
A string index signature requires all explicitly defined properties to match its return type, but 'id' is a string instead of a number.
The index property key type must be number when named properties exist.
Index signatures can only return object or union types, not primitive numbers.
quiz.explanation: A string index signature enforces that all explicitly defined properties match the index signature's return type. Because Dictionary has `[key: string]: number`, every named property must have a type compatible with `number`. Saying that named properties are not allowed with string index signatures is incorrect, as named properties can be combined with index signatures as long as their types align.
quiz.objective: Define index signatures for dictionary structures with consistent return types

quiz.stem: Given the function `function configure(opts: { timeout: number }): void {}`, why does `configure({ timeout: 1000, extra: true })` produce a compiler error, while `const conf = { timeout: 1000, extra: true }; configure(conf);` succeeds?
options: Object literals undergo excess property checking when passed directly, whereas assigning the literal to an intermediate variable bypasses excess property checks.
Intermediate variables automatically discard any properties that do not match the function parameter type at runtime.
Functions only check parameter types when called with object literals and completely disable type checking for variables.
The compiler implicitly asserts intermediate variables as `any` when they are passed as function arguments.
quiz.explanation: Passing an object literal directly triggers excess property checks, rejecting properties not present on the target type. Assigning the object literal to an intermediate variable first bypasses excess property checks as long as at least one common property exists. The compiler does not discard properties at runtime or turn intermediate variables into `any`.
quiz.objective: Debug excess property check errors on object literal assignments using index signatures and intermediate variables

quiz.stem: Which of the following property types is permitted for an index signature key in TypeScript?
options: boolean
object
symbol
Function
quiz.explanation: Supported index signature key types are string, number, symbol, template string patterns, or union types composed purely of these. Types like boolean, object, or Function are not permitted as index signature key types.
quiz.objective: Define index signatures for dictionary structures with consistent return types

lessons.title: Function Signatures, Promises, and Special Return Types
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons established how to define object shapes and request configurations using interfaces with optional and index properties. We also set up TypeScript's strict type-checking configuration and learned how to export ES modules for Node.js.
lessons.explanation:
Function parameter type annotations are written immediately following the parameter name to indicate the acceptable types of inputs [c:a153b7008a17]. Function return type annotations are positioned directly after the function parameter list [c:b608026cc420]. When annotating the return type of a function that returns a promise, use the Promise type [c:30bf7f2e5cb9]. An async function returning a number can be explicitly annotated with a return type of Promise<number> [c:b207b58ed6cc].

In a function type expression, parameter names are required; omitting a parameter name and writing only a type name makes the identifier become the parameter name typed as any [c:71fc9a87f417]. The void type indicates the return type of functions that do not return a value, and it is automatically inferred when return statements return no explicit value or are absent [c:0ef617cce3bd]. A function defined literally with a void return type annotation is forbidden from returning any value [c:3703d503d9c2]. A function that is contextually typed with a void return type is permitted to return a value, but that returned value is ignored [c:29be3cbb7d77].

The unknown type can hold any value, but unlike any, TypeScript does not allow operations to be performed on unknown values without narrowing [c:56b18e7f4661]. The never return type signifies that a function never finishes normally, such as when throwing an exception or terminating the program [c:7ca746af17e2].

exercise.task:
In client.ts, complete four functions for an API client library:
1. fail(message: string): Annotate its return type as never and throw an Error with the given message.
2. parsePayload(raw: unknown): Annotate the raw parameter as unknown and return type as string. If raw is a string, return it; otherwise return JSON.stringify(raw).
3. logResponse(message: string, logger: (msg: string) => void): Annotate logger as a function taking msg: string and returning void, with logResponse returning void. In the body, call logger(message).
4. fetchStatus(endpoint: string): Annotate the return type as Promise<number>. If endpoint does not start with '/', call fail('Invalid endpoint'); otherwise return 200.
hints: In TypeScript, functions that throw without returning normally must be annotated with the return type `never`.
In callback type signatures like `(msg: string) => void`, the parameter name (`msg`) is required; writing just `(string) => void` would create a parameter named `string` with type `any`.
For async functions, wrap the resolved type in `Promise<...>`, such as `Promise<number>`.

options: Promise<number>
number
Promise<void>
async number
quiz.explanation: Because async functions return promises in JavaScript, the return type must be annotated with the Promise type wrapping the value type, giving Promise<number>. Annotating with number is rejected because an async function returns a Promise object, not an immediate number. Promise<void> incorrectly declares that no value is resolved, and async number is invalid TypeScript syntax.
quiz.objective: Annotate function parameters, return values, and asynchronous Promise return types

quiz.stem: You want to declare a callback function type that accepts a string argument and returns no value. What happens if you define the parameter type as `(string) => void` instead of `(message: string) => void`?
options: TypeScript treats string as the parameter name and gives it an inferred type of any.
TypeScript treats string as the type and generates an anonymous positional parameter.
TypeScript raises a compile-time syntax error requiring parameter names to precede colons.
TypeScript reverses the definition and treats string as the return type.
quiz.explanation: In a function type expression, parameter names are required. If you omit the parameter name and write only (string) => void, TypeScript parses 'string' as the identifier name of the parameter and gives it the type any. Believing that TypeScript treats it as an anonymous positional parameter of type string is a common misconception.
quiz.objective: Specify function types using void, unknown, and never for callbacks, untyped inputs, and terminal error functions

quiz.stem: An API client library contains a function `crash(reason: string)` that logs a message and unconditionally throws an `Error` to stop program execution. What is the correct return type annotation for `crash`?
options: never, because the function never finishes execution normally.
void, because the function does not return an explicit value.
unknown, because the thrown error may be of any arbitrary type.
void, because never is only permitted for infinite loops.
quiz.explanation: The never return type signifies that a function never finishes normally, which includes functions that unconditionally throw an exception or terminate execution. While void indicates a function that finishes normally without returning a value, crash never finishes normally. The unknown option confuses the returned value with a caught error, and never is valid for exceptions as well as infinite loops.
quiz.objective: Specify function types using void, unknown, and never for callbacks, untyped inputs, and terminal error functions

lessons.title: Generic Functions and Type Constraints
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons established that TypeScript uses interfaces to describe object shapes and contracts for HTTP requests and responses. We also learned how function parameters and return types enforce specific values and structures at compile time.
lessons.explanation:
A generic type parameter constraint can be defined by using an interface along with the `extends` keyword on the type variable [c:21af8fc9cbae]. An `extends` clause can be used in a generic function to constrain a type parameter to a specific subset of types [c:884b13fb3aab]. The type of a generic function lists the type parameters first, followed by parameter and return types [c:c01aa516d144].

When calling a generic function, the TypeScript compiler can automatically infer the type argument based on the argument passed in [c:dedb5cb9abbf]. Constraining a generic type parameter to a shape does not allow returning an arbitrary object matching that constraint if the return type is typed as the parameter itself [c:07de23982fb8]. Default types for a type parameter must satisfy any constraint specified on that type parameter [c:f5bd37b7b1ac].

A generic parameter can be moved to the whole interface so that it is visible to all members and locked in when the interface type argument is specified [c:bf92e4986de7]. In addition, a type parameter can be constrained by another type parameter, such as ensuring a key exists on an object type using `extends keyof` [c:6c2b0d4e64f5].

exercise.task:
In `repository.ts`:
1. Update the `EntityStore<T>` interface so that its type parameter `T` is constrained to types implementing `Identifiable` using `extends`.
2. Implement `updateRecord<T extends Identifiable>(record: T): T` as a generic function constrained by `Identifiable` that returns the passed record.
3. Implement `getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(item: T, key: K): T[K]` with type parameters constrained using `extends keyof` so that it returns `item[key]`.
hints: Use the `extends` keyword after a type parameter to constrain it to a shape or interface, such as `<T extends Identifiable>`.
To ensure a property key belongs to an object type, constrain a second type parameter using `K extends keyof T`.
In `getProperty`, write the signature as `<T, K extends keyof T>(item: T, key: K): T[K]` and return `item[key]`.

options: The function promises to return the specific type T passed by the caller, which may contain additional properties beyond id, not just an arbitrary object matching the constraint.
Type parameter constraints using extends are only permitted on interface declarations and cannot be applied to generic function parameters.
Type parameter constraints require a default type argument to be specified whenever an extends clause is present.
The return value must be explicitly cast to HasId with 'as HasId' because T cannot be resolved without a type assertion.
quiz.explanation: Constraining a generic type parameter to a shape does not allow returning an arbitrary object matching that constraint if the return type is typed as the parameter itself [c:07de23982fb8]. The caller promises a concrete `T` (which might have fields like `name` or `role`), and returning `{ id: "default-id" }` fails to satisfy those additional properties. The option claiming constraints only work on interfaces is incorrect because `extends` can constrain generic functions [c:884b13fb3aab]. The option claiming defaults are required is incorrect because constraints do not require defaults. Casting to `HasId` would still fail because the promised return type is `T`.
quiz.objective: Write generic functions and generic types with type parameter constraints using extends

options: Type 'K' cannot be used to index type 'T' because K is unconstrained and is not guaranteed to be a key of T.
Generic functions in TypeScript cannot declare more than one type parameter within angle brackets.
The indexed access type T[K] is only supported if record is typed as Record<string, unknown>.
The compiler cannot infer type arguments for K unless a default type is assigned in the signature.
quiz.explanation: A type parameter can be constrained by another type parameter using extends keyof to ensure a key exists on an object type [c:6c2b0d4e64f5]. Without `K extends keyof T`, `K` is completely unconstrained, so TypeScript cannot guarantee that `key` exists on `record` and rejects `T[K]` and `record[key]`. The option stating functions cannot have multiple type parameters is incorrect because TypeScript allows multiple parameters. The option regarding `Record<string, unknown>` is incorrect because indexed access `T[K]` works directly with constrained parameters. The option regarding default types is incorrect because TypeScript infers type arguments automatically from arguments [c:dedb5cb9abbf].
quiz.objective: Constrain a generic type parameter to valid keys of another type using extends keyof

options: Default types for a type parameter must satisfy any constraint specified on that type parameter.
Default types override and bypass any extends constraint on the type parameter.
Generic type parameter constraints with extends forbid providing default type arguments.
The default type argument must match the constraint interface identically without adding extra properties.
quiz.explanation: Default types for a type parameter must satisfy any constraint specified on that type parameter [c:f5bd37b7b1ac]. Because `{ id: string; name: string }` possesses an `id: string` property, it satisfies `{ id: string }`. The option claiming defaults bypass constraints is incorrect because constraints are always enforced. The option stating extends forbids defaults is incorrect. The option requiring identical properties without extras is incorrect because any subtype satisfying the constraint shape is permitted.
quiz.objective: Write generic functions and generic types with type parameter constraints using extends

lessons.title: Narrowing with Runtime Type Guards
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons introduced union types and optional properties for representing values that can take multiple shapes. We also saw functions accepting unknown or union inputs, requiring validation before safely accessing specific properties.
lessons.explanation:
Narrowing occurs when TypeScript deduces a more specific type for a value based on the structure of the code [c:8712b4f85b5b]. In TypeScript, checking against the string returned by JavaScript's typeof operator acts as a type guard [c:d2c11738d755]. TypeScript expects typeof to return one of eight string values: 'string', 'number', 'bigint', 'boolean', 'symbol', 'undefined', 'object', or 'function' [c:79614b5b565f]. A union type can be narrowed by checking the JavaScript typeof operator against a type name such as 'string' [c:35458699cdc2].

JavaScript has a historical quirk where typeof null evaluates to 'object' [c:15f871bd6fb5]. Because typeof null evaluates to 'object', narrowing with typeof strs === 'object' on a union like string | string[] | null leaves null in the type [c:15f871bd6fb5]. To remove null safely, a union type containing null can be narrowed by performing an equality check against null [c:a8c5ec38f207]. Furthermore, checking loosely whether a value is not equal to null using != null narrows out both null and undefined from the type [c:61a4217407ee]. Checking for undefined using an inequality check narrows an optional property to its defined type [c:eb7f88f77f85].

TypeScript also uses switch statements and equality operators including ===, !==, ==, and != to narrow types [c:b3018a1825f0]. In conditionals, values like 0, NaN, the empty string, 0n, null, and undefined coerce to false, while all other values coerce to true [c:0ea711d89d16]. Boolean negations using the ! operator filter out truthy types from the negated branches [c:401e21368e68]. Double-boolean negation (!!) causes TypeScript to infer a literal boolean type true on truthy values, whereas the Boolean function infers the broader boolean type [c:3473ba6b7cb1].

When dealing with objects in a union, JavaScript's in operator provides another narrowing tool [c:b2a674057546]. Using the in operator to test 'value' in x narrows the true branch to union types with an optional or required property named value, and the false branch to types with an optional or missing property [c:b2a674057546].

exercise.task:
In `payload.ts`, implement two functions that safely narrow union types:
1. `formatPayload(payload: string | number | string[] | null): string`: 
   - If `payload === null`, return `"none"`.
   - If `typeof payload === "number"`, return `payload.toFixed(2)`.
   - If `typeof payload === "string"`, check truthiness: if it is empty (`!payload`), return `"empty string"`; otherwise return `payload.trim()`.
   - Otherwise (`payload` is `string[]`), join the items with `", "`.
2. `extractData(response: { error: string } | { data: string }): string`: 
   - Use the `in` operator to check if `"error"` is in `response`. If so, return `"Error: " + response.error`.
   - Otherwise, return response.data.
hints: Remember that typeof null is 'object', so test for null with `payload === null` before relying on object or array operations.
Check `typeof payload === 'number'` and `typeof payload === 'string'`. In the string branch, use `if (!payload)` to detect the empty string.
For `extractData`, use `if ('error' in response)` to let TypeScript narrow `response` to `{ error: string }` in the true branch.

quiz.stem: Why does checking `typeof value === 'object'` fail to narrow a `string[] | null` union down to just `string[]`?
options: In JavaScript, `typeof null` evaluates to the string `'object'`, so `null` remains in the narrowed union.
TypeScript ignores `typeof` guards unless the value is strictly an object literal.
TypeScript requires `Array.isArray()` to be invoked before any `typeof` operator can be parsed.
JavaScript considers `null` to be undefined unless strict mode is enabled in the compiler.
quiz.explanation: Because typeof null evaluates to 'object' in JavaScript, narrowing with typeof strs === 'object' on a union containing null leaves null in the type. The option stating that TypeScript ignores typeof guards is wrong because typeof is a recognized built-in type guard.
quiz.objective: Explain why typeof null evaluates to 'object' and how to safely narrow null from object unions

quiz.stem: You have a variable `input` with type `string | null | undefined`. Which check safely narrows `input` to just `string` in a single comparison?
options: input != null
typeof input === 'object'
input === null
input !== undefined
quiz.explanation: Checking loosely whether a value is not equal to null using != null narrows out both null and undefined from the type, leaving string. In contrast, checking input !== undefined leaves null in the type, and input === null only tests specifically for null.
quiz.objective: Narrow union types using typeof, truthiness checks, equality checks, and the in operator

quiz.stem: A function receives `response: { success: boolean; data: string } | { success: boolean; error: string }`. How can TypeScript narrow to the error branch?
options: By checking if ('error' in response)
By checking typeof response === 'error'
By checking response.error != null directly without narrowing
By calling response.hasProperty('error')
quiz.explanation: Using the in operator to test 'error' in response narrows the true branch to types with that property. Checking typeof response === 'error' is invalid because typeof never returns 'error', and accessing response.error before narrowing causes a compiler error because 'error' is not guaranteed to exist on both union members.
quiz.objective: Narrow union types using typeof, truthiness checks, equality checks, and the in operator

lessons.title: User-Defined Type Guards and Predicates
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons showed how TypeScript narrows types inside conditional blocks using standard JavaScript checks like typeof and the in operator. We also saw that network responses and unvalidated payloads often enter an application typed as unknown, requiring validation before accessing properties.
lessons.explanation:
A user-defined type guard function uses a type predicate as its return type annotation [c:08a1e463f5f6]. A return type predicate must follow the syntax parameterName is Type, referencing a parameter from the function's signature [c:1a8016768f9f].

When a user-defined type guard with parameterName is Type is used in an if/else check, TypeScript narrows the variable to the specified type in the if branch and eliminates that type in the else branch [c:4b274888d1f8].

exercise.task:
In guards.ts, implement two user-defined type guard functions: `isUser(data: unknown): data is User` and `isPost(data: unknown): data is Post`.

1. Annotate `isUser` with the return type predicate `data is User`. It must return `true` only when `data` is a non-null object with an `id` property of type `number` and a `name` property of type `string`.
2. Annotate `isPost` with the return type predicate `data is Post`. It must return `true` only when `data` is a non-null object with an `id` property of type `number`, a `title` property of type `string`, and an `authorId` property of type `number`.
hints: Remember that a type predicate has the form `parameterName is TargetType` instead of `boolean` in the function's return signature.
Check `typeof data === "object" && data !== null` first before using the `in` operator to verify properties exist on the object.
Once you know the properties exist using `"prop" in data`, verify each property's runtime type with `typeof data.prop === "number"` or `typeof data.prop === "string"`.

quiz.stem: You are writing a function to validate API responses of unknown structure before passing them to a renderer: `function isValidUser(data: unknown)`. What return type annotation must you provide so that TypeScript narrows `data` to `User` inside an `if (isValidUser(data))` block?
options: data is User
boolean
User
data: User
quiz.explanation: A user-defined type guard requires a return type predicate of the form `parameterName is Type`, so `data is User` tells TypeScript to narrow `data` to `User` when the check returns true. Annotating with `boolean` only informs TypeScript that a truth value was returned without performing narrowing. Annotating with `User` would mean the function returns a `User` object itself, not a validation boolean.
quiz.objective: Write user-defined type guard functions returning type predicates (parameterName is Type) to validate unknown API inputs

options: The predicate parameter name `item` does not match the function parameter name `response`.
Type predicates cannot use `unknown` as the parameter type.
The keyword `is` can only be used with classes, not interfaces like `Post`.
The function must return an explicit `Post` instance rather than a boolean expression.
quiz.explanation: A return type predicate must follow the syntax `parameterName is Type`, where `parameterName` must match the name of a parameter from the function's signature. In this function, the parameter is named `response`, so the predicate must be `response is Post` rather than `item is Post`.
quiz.objective: Write user-defined type guard functions returning type predicates (parameterName is Type) to validate unknown API inputs

quiz.stem: You have a union type `type Content = TextContent | ImageContent` and a type guard `function isText(content: Content): content is TextContent`. How does TypeScript treat `content` inside the `else` branch of `if (isText(content)) { ... } else { ... }`?
options: TypeScript narrows `content` to `ImageContent` by eliminating `TextContent`.
TypeScript keeps `content` typed as the full `TextContent | ImageContent` union.
TypeScript treats `content` as `never` because guards only evaluate true branches.
TypeScript widens `content` to `unknown` because the guard returned false.
quiz.explanation: When a type guard with `parameterName is Type` is used in an `if/else` check, TypeScript narrows the variable to `Type` in the `if` branch and eliminates that type in the `else` branch. Eliminating `TextContent` from `TextContent | ImageContent` leaves `ImageContent` in the `else` branch.
quiz.objective: Write user-defined type guard functions returning type predicates (parameterName is Type) to validate unknown API inputs

lessons.title: Discriminated Unions and Exhaustive Checks
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons established how TypeScript narrows union types using control flow analysis and custom type predicates. We also saw how checking object shapes helps refine general types into specific structures.
lessons.explanation:
When every type within a union contains a shared property with literal types, TypeScript recognizes it as a discriminated union and can narrow out members of the union [c:678bdbb4f080]. Discriminated union members can be narrowed in both if checks and switch statements by checking their discriminant property [c:691353716742].

When narrowing reduces a union's possibilities so completely that no types remain, TypeScript represents that unreachable state with the never type [c:0ab8e5c3250f] [c:e7929deb6d56]. The never type can be assigned to every type, but no type other than never itself is assignable to never [c:409f4a7e8e4b].

Narrowing can be combined with assigning to a never-typed variable in a switch statement's default branch to achieve exhaustive checking [c:14878bfc087a]. Exhaustive checking in a switch statement can be enforced by assigning the unhandled discriminated union variable to a const typed as never in the default case [c:489e705357aa]. Adding an unhandled case to a discriminated union that has an exhaustive check assigning to never will cause a TypeScript compile error [c:b04f53a12c6a].

exercise.task:
Model an API response as a discriminated union and implement an exhaustive switch statement.

1. In `api.ts`, update `SuccessResponse<T>` so that its discriminant `status` has the literal type `"success"` and includes `data: T`.
2. Update `ErrorResponse` so that its discriminant `status` has the literal type `"error"` and includes `error: string`.
3. Implement `formatResponse<T>(response: ApiResponse<T>): string` using a `switch (response.status)`:
   - When `"loading"`: return `"Loading..."`
   - When `"success"`: return `"Data: " + JSON.stringify(response.data)`
   - When `"error"`: return `"Error: " + response.error`
   - In the `default` branch: enforce exhaustive checking by assigning `response` to a constant typed as `never` (`const _exhaustiveCheck: never = response;`) and return `_exhaustiveCheck`.
hints: Use literal types like status: "success" instead of the broad string type so TypeScript can use status as a discriminant.
In the switch statement, each case label ("loading", "success", "error") narrows response so you can directly access response.data or response.error.
In the default block, assign response to a variable explicitly annotated with type never: const _exhaustiveCheck: never = response; return _exhaustiveCheck;

options: The discriminant property `type` was given the broad type `string` rather than a literal type like `"login"`, preventing TypeScript from identifying it as a discriminated union.
Interfaces cannot form discriminated unions; only type aliases declared with `type` can have discriminant properties.
TypeScript only recognizes discriminated unions if the common property is named `kind` rather than `type`.
The union members must be converted into runtime classes before narrowing can take effect.
quiz.explanation: TypeScript recognizes a discriminated union when every member contains a shared property with literal types. When `type` is annotated as `string`, it is a general string rather than a literal type, so narrowing does not occur. Interfaces work seamlessly in unions, and any shared property name can serve as the discriminant.
quiz.objective: Construct discriminated unions with common literal discriminant properties

options: TypeScript raises a compile error in the `default` branch because `notification` has narrowed to `PushNotification`, which is not assignable to `never`.
TypeScript silently compiles and skips the `default` case at runtime whenever a `PushNotification` is encountered.
TypeScript raises an error at the `switch` header because switch statements over unions cannot have a `default` case.
TypeScript converts `PushNotification` to `any` in the default branch, deferring any error until runtime.
quiz.explanation: Because `PushNotification` is not handled in any preceding `case`, `notification` retains the type `PushNotification` when control reaches `default`. Because no type other than `never` is assignable to `never`, attempting to assign `notification` to `_exhaustiveCheck: never` triggers a compile-time error.
quiz.objective: Enforce compile-time exhaustive switch checking over discriminated unions using the never type in the default case

quiz.stem: Why does assigning the switch subject to a variable of type `never` in the default case guarantee exhaustive checking at compile time?
options: Narrowing removes each handled variant until no possibilities remain, producing `never`; if any variant is unhandled, it retains that variant's type, which cannot be assigned to `never`.
The `never` type instructs the TypeScript compiler to automatically generate code for unhandled variants during compilation.
All types in TypeScript can be assigned to `never`, allowing the compiler to perform a runtime assertion.
Assigning to `never` causes JavaScript to throw a runtime SyntaxError when an unhandled case is encountered.
quiz.explanation: When narrowing eliminates every variant in a union, TypeScript uses `never` to represent the remaining unreachable state. Since no type except `never` itself can be assigned to `never`, any unhandled variant will fail type-checking if assigned to a `never`-typed constant. It does not generate code or alter runtime behavior.
quiz.objective: Enforce compile-time exhaustive switch checking over discriminated unions using the never type in the default case

lessons.title: ES Modules with Types and Values
lessons.recall: In previous lessons, we created domain interfaces such as User and Post alongside custom type guards like isUser and isPost to safely validate unknown data at runtime. We also defined generic discriminated union types like ApiResponse to represent asynchronous loading, success, and error states. Now we will organize these types, guards, and utilities into reusable modules using ECMAScript Module syntax.
lessons.explanation:
ECMAScript Modules (ESM) are built into JavaScript and provide dedicated import and export syntax to share code across files [c:95ed3eecfc62]. In TypeScript, any file with a top-level import or export declaration is treated as a module [c:a208206e7b9c].

Variables, functions, and classes can be exported individually without the default keyword and imported using curly braces [c:2f9c67da7603]. Specific named bindings can be imported from an ES Module using curly braces enclosing the binding name [c:5e50ee6ec0dd]. TypeScript types and interfaces can be exported and imported using the standard ES Module syntax used for values [c:3ae4c75a145c]. Type aliases, interfaces, enums, and namespaces can be exported using an export modifier or referenced alongside JavaScript declarations in named export lists [c:5f30ff0d1b9c]. Exported types and other TypeScript declarations can be imported using standard ECMAScript import syntax [c:35b55dc83698].

Imported identifiers can be renamed using the `as` keyword [c:fef8c3f4bb50]. All exports from a module can be imported into a single namespace object using the `* as` syntax [c:541d7f0970b2]. When using namespace imports or exports, exported types can be accessed on the namespace when used in a type position [c:164986515b64].

A file can specify its primary export using the `export default` syntax [c:02456c36cfbb]. In ES Module syntax, a module can define a default export using the `export default` keywords [c:1a45976b45fb]. Default and named imports can be combined in a single import statement [c:6862d141ac52]. Furthermore, a module can re-export all exports from another module using the `export * from` syntax [c:f54f548d7754].

exercise.task:
Organize your web app's domain code into modules and expose them through a clean barrel entry point:
1. In `service.ts`, complete the default export function `renderUserResponse(response: ApiResponse<User>): ServiceResult`. It should compute `formatted` using `formatResponse(response)`, and compute `valid` as `true` only if `response.status === "success"` and `isUser(response.data)` is `true` (otherwise `false`).
2. In `index.ts`, use wildcard re-exports (`export * from ...`) to re-export all exports from `./guards.ts`, `./api.ts`, and `./service.ts`.
3. In `index.ts`, re-export the default export from `./service.ts` as the default export of `index.ts`.
hints: In service.ts, check that response.status === 'success' and call isUser(response.data) to set the boolean valid flag.
Use `export * from './guards.ts';` and `export * from './api.ts';` to wildcard re-export both files from index.ts.
To re-export a default export in a barrel file, you can write `export { default } from './service.ts';` alongside `export * from './service.ts';`.

quiz.stem: A module `types.ts` defines `export interface User { id: string; }` and `export const DEFAULT_USER: User = { id: "guest" };`. In another file, which statement correctly imports both the interface and the object value using standard ES module syntax?
options: import { User, DEFAULT_USER } from "./types.js";
import User, { DEFAULT_USER } from "./types.js";
import { interface User, const DEFAULT_USER } from "./types.js";
import * as User from "./types.js";
quiz.explanation: TypeScript types and values can be imported together using standard named import syntax with curly braces: `import { User, DEFAULT_USER } from "./types.js";`. The option `import User, { DEFAULT_USER } from "./types.js";` is incorrect because `User` was not declared with `export default`. The option `import { interface User, const DEFAULT_USER } from "./types.js";` is invalid syntax because declaration keywords (`interface`, `const`) cannot appear inside an import specifier clause. The option `import * as User from "./types.js";` imports the entire module as a single namespace object rather than importing the individual bindings.
quiz.objective: Export and import functions, objects, and type definitions using standard ES Module syntax

quiz.stem: You are creating a centralized entry-point `index.ts` file for a domain package. You want to expose all functions, constants, and types defined in `./validators.ts` as part of the public API without importing and naming each one individually. Which syntax accomplishes this?
options: export * from "./validators.js";
import * from "./validators.js";
export default from "./validators.js";
export { * as all } from "./validators.js";
quiz.explanation: The wildcard re-export syntax `export * from "./validators.js";` exports all named bindings and types from the target module into the current module's public exports. The option `import * from "./validators.js";` is invalid syntax because namespace imports require `* as name`. The option `export default from "./validators.js";` is not valid ECMAScript syntax and would only target a default export. The option `export { * as all } from "./validators.js";` nests all exports under an `all` object rather than exposing them directly at the top level of the public API.
quiz.objective: Organize module public APIs using named exports, default exports, and wildcard re-exports

quiz.stem: A module `logger.ts` declares a primary function with `export default function log(msg: string): void` and also exports a helper `export function formatLog(msg: string): string`. In `server.ts`, how can you import both functions in a single statement?
options: import log, { formatLog } from "./logger.js";
import { log, formatLog } from "./logger.js";
import log and { formatLog } from "./logger.js";
import * as log, { formatLog } from "./logger.js";
quiz.explanation: Default and named imports can be combined in a single import statement by placing the default import before the comma and the curly braces for named imports: `import log, { formatLog } from "./logger.js";`. The option `import { log, formatLog } from "./logger.js";` fails because `log` was exported as a default export, not as a named export. The option `import log and { formatLog } from "./logger.js";` is invalid syntax because ES module syntax separates import clauses with commas, not the word `and`. The option `import * as log, { formatLog } from "./logger.js";` is invalid syntax because namespace imports cannot be combined with named import brackets.
quiz.objective: Organize module public APIs using named exports, default exports, and wildcard re-exports

lessons.title: Type-Only Imports and Bundler Optimization
lessons.recall: Earlier lessons demonstrated how to define entity interfaces and type guards in dedicated modules, and how to import them into service files. You also learned how discriminated unions narrow response types across API handling boundaries.
lessons.explanation:
An `import type` declaration restricts the statement to only importing types [c:563e9340b3b5]. Even values can be imported with `import type`, but because they will not exist in emitted JavaScript, they can only be referenced in non-emitting type positions [c:1208b07a5282]. Using an identifier imported via `import type` as a value causes a TypeScript compiler error [c:d285d8142a6e].

A type-only import declaration cannot specify both a default import and named bindings together because of ambiguity over what the `type` keyword modifies [c:d73b33dfab81].

Individual imports within a statement can be prefixed with `type` to declare inline type imports [c:a3b5666d9b1e]. Type-only imports and inline type imports enable transpilers like Babel, swc, and esbuild to recognize which imports can be safely stripped [c:95076a38c20a]. Import declarations using `import type`, exports using `export type { ... }`, and individual specifiers prefixed with `type` are guaranteed to be elided from compiled JavaScript [c:7c63361430a6].

exercise.task: In `service.ts`, fix the import from `./guards.ts` so runtime guard functions (`isUser` and `isPost`) are imported as values, while entity interfaces (`User` and `Post`) are imported as inline types. Then implement `renderPostResponse` to validate that `response.status === "success" && isPost(response.data)` and format the response using `formatResponse(response)`.
hints: Check which specifiers in the `./guards.ts` import statement are functions called at runtime versus interfaces used as types.

An inline type import prefixes an identifier with `type` (such as `type Post`). Runtime functions like `isPost` must not have the `type` prefix, otherwise they are stripped and cannot be used as values.
In `service.ts`, change `type isPost` to `isPost` in the import list from `./guards.ts`, and set `formatted: formatResponse(response)` in `renderPostResponse`.

options: `validateToken` was imported with the inline `type` modifier, which restricts it to non-emitting type positions and causes a compiler error when used as a value.
The compiler cannot infer the return type of `validateToken` without an explicit type parameter in the function declaration.
Inline `type` imports are restricted to interface and type alias identifiers and cannot be placed before function names.
Module `./auth.ts` must export `validateToken` as a `default` export when consumed alongside type-only specifiers.
quiz.explanation: Prefixing an individual import specifier with `type` declares an inline type import. Values imported with `type` do not exist in emitted JavaScript and can only be used in non-emitting type positions; using them in a runtime value position produces a compiler error. The compiler does allow the `type` keyword before functions, but restricts their subsequent use to types.
quiz.objective: Debug compiler errors caused by using identifiers imported via import type in runtime value positions

quiz.stem: You are building a client utility that needs the runtime helper `sendRequest` and the interface `RequestConfig` from `./client.ts`. You want a single import statement where tools like esbuild or swc can safely elide `RequestConfig` without stripping `sendRequest`. Which declaration accomplishes this?
options: import { sendRequest, type RequestConfig } from "./client.ts";
import type { sendRequest, RequestConfig } from "./client.ts";
import { sendRequest, RequestConfig as type } from "./client.ts";
import type { sendRequest } and { RequestConfig } from "./client.ts";
quiz.explanation: TypeScript allows individual imports within an import statement to be prefixed with `type` (inline type imports). This informs transpilers that `RequestConfig` is purely a type to be elided, while `sendRequest` is a runtime value that must be preserved. Using `import type` for the entire statement would turn `sendRequest` into a type-only reference that cannot be called at runtime.
quiz.objective: Declare type-only imports (import type) and inline type imports to distinguish types from runtime values

quiz.stem:
A developer attempts to combine a default import and named type specifiers in a type-only import declaration:

```ts
import type Client, { ClientOptions } from "./client.ts";
```

Why does the TypeScript compiler disallow this statement?
options: A type-only import declaration cannot specify both a default import and named bindings together because it is ambiguous whether `type` applies to the default import or the entire declaration.
The `import type` keyword can only be applied to named import clauses enclosed in curly braces, never default imports.
TypeScript requires all default imports to be runtime values and cannot elide default exports during bundling.
Bundlers like esbuild require default type imports to use `import { default as Client }` instead.
quiz.explanation: A type-only import declaration (`import type`) cannot declare both a default import and named bindings together because the syntax creates ambiguity over whether `type` applies to just the default import or the entire import statement. To import both, developers separate them into distinct declarations or use inline `type` imports.
quiz.objective: Declare type-only imports (import type) and inline type imports to distinguish types from runtime values
